chunks: "A feedforward capacitor is a small capacitor placed across the upper resistor of the output feedback divider, from V out to the feedback pin.
At DC it does nothing, because the capacitor is open and the divider ratio sets the output voltage.
At higher frequency it shorts out R1, so the feedback signal follows V out more directly, with no divider attenuation.
That makes a lead network: a zero at 1 over 2 pi R1 Cff, and a pole at 1 over 2 pi times R1 in parallel with R2 times Cff.
Between them the phase advances, with a peak lead that depends on the ratio of the pole to zero, which is V out over V ref.
So it gives me extra phase margin right around the crossover frequency, if I choose Cff so that the zero is below and the pole above crossover.
It also lets the loop see output changes faster, so the transient response improves.
I'd use it when the output has only ceramic capacitors, which have no ESR zero to give lead, when the phase margin is low or the part's datasheet recommends it, or to speed up a slow response.
The trade-off is that at high frequency the feedback gain goes up by V out over V ref, so switching ripple and noise get coupled directly to the FB pin, which can add jitter.
Too large a Cff makes this worse, and it only helps if the output voltage is much higher than the reference. For a 3. 3 volts output from a 0.
8 volts reference that's a 12 decibels boost."
